titulo: SMO: service-based architecture and the SMOSs
resumo: This lesson opens the management and orchestration course by introducing the SMO (Service Management and Orchestration), the layer that makes a multi-vendor, disaggregated Open RAN network with hundreds of sites operable. You see what the SMO does (collect, consolidate, analyze, apply policies, orchestrate and monitor), how it connects to the network through O1, O2, A1 and the Open Fronthaul M-Plane, and how it is organized as a service-based architecture, with functions (SMOF) that expose services (SMOS). It then walks through each SMOS with its step-by-step scenarios (SME, DME, RAN NF OAM, NFO, FOCOM, TE&IV, SO, SA, rApp Management, Software Package Onboarding and A1 Related), solves the 'who does what' quizzes, and closes with the four service groups and part 1 of the assessment: studying a real SMO platform.
objetivos: Explain why the SMO exists in a multi-vendor, disaggregated Open RAN environment and describe its cycle of collecting, analyzing, acting and monitoring.
Place the SMO relative to the O1, O2, A1 and Open Fronthaul M-Plane interfaces, the Non-RT RIC, rApps and R1.
Describe the SMO service-based architecture: producer and consumer, SMOF and SMOS, and the four service groups.
Distinguish SME from DME; RAN NF OAM from NFO, FOCOM and TE&IV; SO from SA; and Software Package Onboarding from rApp Management.
Chain the SMOSs through an incident (a degraded O-DU, a slice violating its latency) and recognize that no single service solves the problem alone.
Recognize the scope and deadlines of part 1 of the assessment: the study of an SMO platform.

conceitos.d: An Open RAN network brings together O-RU, O-DU, O-CU, Near-RT RIC (near-real-time RAN Intelligent Controller) and O-Cloud, from several vendors and spread over hundreds of sites. The environment has multiple vendors, disaggregated components, a need for automation, data-driven operation and requires management scalability: this brings openness, interoperability and flexibility, but raises operational complexity, and configuring each component individually does not scale. The SMO exists to reduce that complexity and let the network be operated in a more automated and intelligent way. Its responsibilities: orchestration and management of network services and functions; configuration and inventory; FCAPS (Fault, Configuration, Accounting, Performance, Security); operational automation; policy coordination; integration with data analytics and AI/ML; lifecycle of applications/rApps; unifying the management of heterogeneous components, easing interoperability; and supervising the network centrally.

conceitos.t: What the SMO is and how it connects to the network
conceitos.d: SMO (Service Management and Orchestration) is the management, automation and orchestration layer of the Open RAN architecture, the network's 'operational brain' from the management point of view. It works as a cycle: it collects network data and events, consolidates KPIs, alarms and context, analyzes performance and behavior, applies policies or recommendations, orchestrates changes and monitors the result. In the slide 8 diagram, the Non-RT RIC (non-real-time RIC) sits inside the SMO framework, which reaches the network through O-RAN-defined interfaces: O1 to the O-RAN Network Functions, A1 from the Non-RT RIC to the Near-RT RIC, O2 to the O-Cloud and the Open Fronthaul M-Plane (the fronthaul management plane) to the O-RU. The diagram also shows an external system providing enrichment data to the SMO, Y1 consumers of RAN information, the O-Cloud notification towards the network functions, and the NG interface, defined by 3GPP, to the 5GC.

The SMO is organized as an SBA (Service-Based Architecture): capabilities are exposed as standardized services, and each component acts as a service producer (it exposes an API, hosts a resource or holds data that other parts need) and/or a service consumer (it initiates a request to use the resources or data of another service). Watch out: on slide 10 these two definitions appear swapped relative to their names; here we use the meaning the deck itself applies in the SME and DME flows (slides 16, 17 and 20), where the producer registers and offers and the consumer discovers and uses. In the diagram, the SMOS producers/consumers attach to a common bus, and rApps reach the services through R1, via the R1 Termination inside the Non-RT RIC (the deck only draws R1; by the usual definition it is the interface between rApps and the SMO/Non-RT RIC framework). SBA characteristics: internal interoperability, separation between functions, incremental evolution by modules, clean integration between components, component replacement, vendor specialization and distributed deployment.

conceitos.t: SMO map: SMOF, SMOS and the four service groups
conceitos.d: An SMOF (SMO Function) is an internal SMO entity that provides one or more services; an SMOS (SMO Service) is the standardized set of management, orchestration and automation capabilities it offers. In the deck's words, the SMOF is the actor and the SMOS is the skill exposed by that actor. Slide 13 connects all SMOSs through the SMOS Communication bus: Software Package Onboarding, Service & Slice Subnet Orchestration, Service & Slice Subnet Assurance, Topology & Inventory (TE&IV), AI/ML Workflow, DME and SME on one side; NFO, FOCOM, RAN NF OAM (CM, FM, PM, tracing, logging), RAN Analytics and PMI (Policy Management and Information) on the other. An example Non-RT RIC SMOF holds the rApps, the R1 termination and the two producers anchored in the Non-RT RIC: rApp Management and A1 Related. Leaving the SMO are O2 (NFO and FOCOM to the O-Cloud), Open FH M-plane (RAN NF OAM to the O-RU), O1 (RAN NF OAM to the Near-RT RIC and other O1 nodes) and A1 (A1 Related to the Near-RT RIC); DME and SME also expose data and services to external producers and consumers. Slide 65 groups the SMOSs into four: platform base services (SME, DME); operation and infrastructure (RAN NF OAM, NFO, FOCOM, TE&IV); delivery and assurance (SO, SA); and automation/applications (rApp Management, A1 Related, Software Package Onboarding, AI/ML workflow (AIMLWF), RAN Analytics, PMI). AIMLWF and PMI are only named in the deck; RAN Analytics has no slide of its own, but appears in the scenarios as the one that processes KPIs, generates insights and points to probable causes.

SME (Service Management and Exposure) lets the other SMOSs find each other, authenticate and talk to each other, sustaining the operation of all of them. Functions: service registration (the producer announces that it exists and what it offers); service discovery (the consumer finds which services are available and where to access them); authentication and authorization (what can be accessed and by whom); support for communication between producers and consumers (service mesh, gateway or other means); bootstrap of new services (optional, helps discover the initial endpoints of the SME itself); and producer heartbeat (optional, checks whether a service is still active). The deck's flow, with A = RAN Analytics and B = Policy Management: A comes up in the SMO and registers with the SME; B needs to consume A, queries the SME to discover the right endpoint, and the SME checks B's credentials and permissions; communication happens with the support of the service-based infrastructure. If A goes down and stops sending heartbeats, the SME stops treating it as available and updates the registry, and a new query from B gets A back as unavailable.

conceitos.t: DME: the shared data layer (and how it differs from the SME)
conceitos.d: DME (Data Management and Exposure) gives the SMOSs a common, standardized mechanism for exposing and consuming data. Functions: data type registration (producers state which data exist, their type and how to consume them); data production and collection (SMO functions and rApps publish data for collection); data discovery (consumers find which data types exist and are available); and exposure for consumption (registered/collected data become available to other SMOFs, rApps and authorized external consumers). The deck's scenario: the RAN NF OAM collects O-CU and O-DU performance metrics via O1 and registers with the DME that it produces this data type; RAN Analytics queries the DME, discovers the data, processes the KPIs and generates insights; the SA discovers the same data set and uses data and insights to detect service degradation; an rApp in the Non-RT RIC consumes the data to train or tune its analytics logic and suggest improvements. Difference (slide 24): the SME focuses on services (service registration, service/endpoint discovery, consumption by service/API call, exposes SMO services); the DME focuses on data (data type registration, data type/source discovery, consumption of collected data, exposes SMO data).

conceitos.t: RAN NF OAM: operating, administering and maintaining network functions
conceitos.d: RAN NF OAM (RAN Network Function Operations, Administration and Maintenance) operates, administers and maintains the RAN network functions (NFs); on the SMO map it is the one that speaks O1 to the NFs and Open FH M-plane to the O-RU. Functions: provisioning management (NF configuration with CRUD operations, synchronous and asynchronous, basic and bulk configuration, configuration notifications and model exposure); fault supervision (alarm subscription, notification, clearing, acknowledgement and query); trace management (starting and supervising traces); streaming and file data reporting; software and hardware management of PNFs (Physical Network Functions); and log collection and exposure. Scenario of a degraded O-DU: the OAM collects O-DU information via O1 and exposes it via SME and DME; RAN Analytics detects an anomaly; the SA concludes that the service is degraded; TE&IV reports the cells, functions and resources involved; an rApp in the Non-RT RIC recommends an optimization, which A1 Related turns into a policy sent to the Near-RT RIC via A1; if a persistent configuration change is needed, the SO or another consumer triggers the OAM to reconfigure the NF; if the cause lies in the deployment or the infrastructure, NFO and/or FOCOM step in.

conceitos.t: NFO: deployment and lifecycle of network functions
conceitos.d: NFO (Network Functions Orchestration) decides and coordinates how a network function is started, scaled, recovered, updated and terminated: it orchestrates the deployment and lifecycle of NFs. Functions: initial deployment (instantiate the NF software on the O-Cloud and trigger the creation of the NF Deployments); monitoring of lifecycle operations (check whether a deployment was created, scaled, healed or terminated correctly); deployment location query (which O-Cloud node cluster hosts it); and secure handling of sensitive configuration data. Scenario of rising traffic in a region: the SA detects performance degradation; RAN Analytics confirms a sustained load increase; the SO decides the service needs expansion and uses the NFO for the lifecycle action; FOCOM provides the view of O-Cloud capacity and resources; the NFO uses O2dms to request a scale-out or a new O-DU instance; the O-Cloud executes it; the NFO tracks the status and checks which cluster hosts the instance; the RAN NF OAM configures, monitors and integrates the new function; TE&IV updates inventory and topology; and SME and DME expose the services and the state data. The slide only writes 'O2dms'; the usual expansion is O2 DMS (Deployment Management Services).

FOCOM (Federated O-Cloud Orchestration and Management) manages and orchestrates the infrastructure resources and clusters of the O-Cloud, across one or several O-Clouds (hence 'federated'), from the infrastructure view of the cloud that supports the RAN. Functions: inventory discovery and query (O-Cloud Sites, physical and logical resources, cluster nodes, deployment managers and O-Cloud templates); subscription to change notifications on that inventory; infrastructure and cluster provisioning (create, update and remove resources); and infrastructure monitoring. Scenario of a new O-DU instance to expand a region: the SO identifies the need for expansion; FOCOM queries the O-Cloud to discover sites, available clusters and compatible templates; SO and/or NFO obtain that view; the NFO picks the most suitable cluster and deploys the new O-DU; the OAM starts configuring and monitoring it; TE&IV reflects the new topology; the DME exposes infrastructure and state data; and the SME exposes FOCOM services to authorized consumers.

conceitos.t: TE&IV: topology and inventory as structural context
conceitos.d: TE&IV (Topology Exposure and Inventory Management) maintains, exposes and queries the inventory and topology of resources and their relationships: it is the SMO's source of structural context, knowing what exists in the network and in the cloud, where it is and how it connects. Functions: management of resources and relationships (create, update, remove and report dependencies, support and communication); inventory and topology queries with filters by resource type and geolocation; and change notifications. TE&IV resources include both the RAN and the O-Cloud. Scenario of a metropolitan RAN service spread over several sites and O-Clouds: TE&IV keeps the view of sites, resources and relationships; the SO queries it to see what exists in the region and how it is organized; FOCOM adds the available infrastructure; the NFO deploys the NFs; and the RAN NF OAM starts configuring and monitoring them. Later the SA detects degradation in part of the service, TE&IV locates the site and resources involved, RAN Analytics uses that context to correlate the data, and the SO coordinates the remediation.

conceitos.t: Who handles what: RAN NF OAM, NFO, FOCOM and TE&IV
conceitos.d: The slide 42 table separates the four operation and infrastructure services by focus, actions and timing. RAN NF OAM: focus on operation and FCAPS management of the NF; configures, monitors faults and collects performance, logs, traces and files; acts during operation of an already deployed NF. NFO: focus on deployment and lifecycle of NFs; instantiates, scales, heals, terminates and upgrades; acts before and during the instance lifecycle. FOCOM: focus on O-Cloud infrastructure and clusters; discovers, provisions and monitors O-Cloud resources and inventory information; acts before and during the preparation and management of the infrastructure that will host the NFs. TE&IV: focus on topology and relational inventory of RAN and O-Cloud resources; maintains, queries and notifies relationships between resources; acts continuously, giving structural context to the other SMOSs' actions. Rule of thumb from the quizzes: configuring what already exists is OAM, creating or scaling the instance is NFO, cloud capacity is FOCOM, and 'what is connected to what' is TE&IV. And, as slide 41 answers, no single SMOS is responsible for solving a problem.

conceitos.t: SO: orchestrating the delivery of services and slices
conceitos.d: SO (Service and Slice Subnet Orchestration) orchestrates the delivery of a RAN service and/or a network slice: it coordinates everything that must happen for the service or slice to be delivered end to end. Functions: service or slice execution (receives and executes the order directly or from a higher-level orchestrator); coordination of lifecycle and configuration of one or more RAN NFs, including several NF Deployments; placement decision (where to place the deployments considering service/slice and application requirements, infrastructure capabilities and connectivity between elements); and transport connectivity coordination (asks the transport domain for bandwidth, latency and redundancy). Scenario of an industrial slice with low latency and high reliability: the SO receives the order and analyzes the requirements; TE&IV helps identify topology and resources; FOCOM reports which clusters can support the solution; the SO decides the provisioning; the NFO deploys O-DU and O-CU; the SO coordinates connectivity between these components and the O-RUs; the RAN NF OAM configures the NFs with the slice parameters; the SA monitors whether the requirements are met; RAN Analytics and/or rApps suggest adjustments; and, in case of degradation, the SO coordinates the corrective actions.

conceitos.t: SA: keeping the service or slice in the desired state
conceitos.d: SA (Service and Slice Subnet Assurance) monitors, evaluates and ensures that RAN services and slices remain in the desired state, triggering remediation and escalation when requirements are not met. Functions: intended-state assurance from start-up (with rApps and other SMOSs); monitoring of data from other SMOS producers and rApps; comparison of the current state with the required one (service requirements, operational goals and expected characteristics); and definition of corrective actions together with rApps and SMOSs (change configuration, scale, change connectivity), escalating to the operator or northbound systems when there is no solution. Scenario: an automation slice requires low latency, high reliability and guaranteed minimum throughput; the SA receives the requirements, monitors data from RAN NF OAM, RAN Analytics, TE&IV and rApps and detects latency above the limit; RAN Analytics points to saturation in part of the processing; TE&IV shows the NFs, cells and sites involved; the SA decides the action with the rApp and SMOSs; the SO coordinates the remediation (configuration adjustment by the OAM, NF change by the NFO, infrastructure adjustment by FOCOM); the SA keeps observing and, if the KPIs do not recover, escalates the problem. Slide 51 summary: the SA assures, the SO orchestrates. On that slide the 'Timing' row seems swapped: 'continuous operation, checking whether the service/slice remains in the desired state' sits in the SO column, but it describes the SA of slides 46 to 48.

conceitos.t: rApp Management: the operational manager of rApps
conceitos.d: rApp Management administers rApp instances (automation and optimization applications in the Non-RT RIC/SMO) and manages their lifecycle and operation: it is the operational manager of the SMO's intelligent applications. Functions: lifecycle (instantiate, update and terminate the rApp); configuration of parameters, tuning and instance; fault management (the rApp reports faults of its own and of its communication with other entities); performance management (reports its own performance and that of its communication); and records (timestamped logs and an audit trail of the configuration actions the rApp performs on the network). Scenario of an energy and load optimization rApp: the package is handled beforehand by Software Package Onboarding; rApp Management deploys the instance and applies the initial configuration; the rApp consumes data from the SMO/Non-RT RIC; rApp Management monitors its behavior and identifies a congestion trend, which the SA uses to assess the risk of degradation and the SO uses to coordinate corrective action; if the rApp misbehaves, rApp Management detects the fault, records logs and supports the corrective actions.

conceitos.t: Software Package Onboarding: the secure entry door for software
conceitos.d: Software Package Onboarding admits software packages into the SMO with validation, security verification, artifact extraction and cataloguing. Functions: onboard packages of O-RAN NFs and rApps; validate format and content; verify security (signature, vendor certificates, integrity and authenticity); extract artifacts for the other SMO components; package and artifact catalogue and query; package removal; and state change notifications (onboarded, deprecated, deleted). Scenario of a new energy rApp delivered by a vendor: a consumer of the service identifies the external package; onboarding receives it, validates it, checks its security and, if valid, unpacks and catalogues it; the DME publishes the package-added event; rApp Management queries the package and uses the artifacts to deploy the rApp, which starts operating in the Non-RT RIC; if it is discontinued, the package moves to the DEPRECATED state, consumers are notified and, with no registered use, the rApp is deleted. Difference (slide 61): onboarding handles NF and rApp packages before operational use (extract, validate, verify security, catalogue); rApp Management handles the running instance during its operational life (deploy, configure, monitor, update, terminate).

conceitos.t: A1 Related: the bridge to the Near-RT RIC over A1
conceitos.d: A1 Related manages A1 policies and AI/ML training support between the SMO/Non-RT RIC and the Near-RT RIC; it is the strategic bridge for RAN optimization over the A1 interface. While rApps generate intelligence and decisions in the Non-RT RIC/SMO, it translates them into structured interaction with the Near-RT RIC. Functions: A1 policy management (discover the policies and policy types available in the Near-RT RICs, policy CRUD, status queries and subscription to event notifications about policies and policy types); AI/ML model training support (discover training capabilities exposed by the Near-RT RICs, request training and query its status); and change notifications (slide 62 repeats the TE&IV sentence here). Scenario of a slice with strict latency and reliability requirements: the SA detects that the slice is approaching an SLA violation; RAN Analytics identifies a degradation trend in certain traffic patterns; an rApp analyzes long-term data and decides the Near-RT RIC should adjust its behavior; A1 Related queries the supported A1 policy types and creates or updates the policy with suitable goals and scope; the Near-RT RIC receives the guidance and adjusts its control over the E2 Nodes; A1 Related queries the enforcement status; and the SA observes the indicators again to see whether the slice is back in the desired state.

Part 1 of the assessment (30% of the grade) is a study of SMO platforms, in groups of up to 5 people, aiming to investigate and analyze an SMO tool or framework for Open RAN networks. Object of study: architecture; SMO services and functions provided; supported O-RAN components; implementation of the O1 and O2 interfaces; management, provisioning and orchestration mechanisms; O-Cloud management capabilities; support for the Network Function lifecycle; and monitoring, telemetry and fault management mechanisms. Deliverables: a 20-minute oral presentation on September 12 (Saturday) and a report on September 15.

formulas.nome: Slice compliance (comparison performed by the SA)
formulas.expr: violation = measured_latency > max_latency; excess = measured_latency - max_latency
formulas.vars: max_latency = slice requirement (e.g., 10 ms); measured_latency = observed value (e.g., 18 ms, that is, 8 ms and 80% above the limit)
formulas.quando: It is the SA's 'comparison of the current state with the required state' (slide 46) applied to the slide 52 scenario; the deck gives the numbers, the expression only makes the comparison explicit.

onde.texto: In our lab, the O-RAN SC SMO (OAM solution) runs in Docker on the Graviton server and covers the RAN NF OAM role: the SDN-R/OpenDaylight controller reads and provisions the simulated O-DU over O1 (NETCONF/YANG), the VES collector publishes faults and measurements to Kafka, and alongside run Keycloak (identity), the ODLUX console and a topology server, with simulated O-DU and O-RU connecting to the SMO through call home. NFO, FOCOM and O2/O-Cloud do not exist here (the O-RAN SC O2 belongs to the INF project), SO, SA and A1 Related are not implemented in this SMO, the Non-RT RIC runs as a separate, non-integrated stack, and the Project 2 OAI gNB has no O1.

quiz.q: I have an Open RAN network with O-DU, O-CU, O-RU, Near-RT RIC, O-Cloud, several vendors and hundreds of sites. Can I simply configure each component individually? Is it efficient?
quiz.a: Open question: there is no closed answer slide, but the following slides indicate that it is not efficient. The Open RAN environment has multiple vendors, disaggregated components, a need for automation, data-driven operation and requires management scalability; this brings openness and flexibility, but raises operational complexity (slide 5). That is why the SMO exists: to reduce complexity, unify the management of heterogeneous components, supervise the network centrally and operate it in a more automated and intelligent way (slide 6).

quiz.q: You are the SMO! An operator has 500 Open RAN sites. During operation: 20 O-DUs show degradation; some sites have high CPU; a new O-DU version must be deployed; a region needs more capacity; the operator wants to track KPIs. What should the SMO do?
quiz.a: Open question, with no answer slide. The deck gives the path: the SMO collects data and events, consolidates KPIs and alarms, analyzes, applies policies, orchestrates changes and monitors the result (slide 8). With the services presented later: the degraded O-DUs are detected with data collected over O1 by the RAN NF OAM and analyzed by RAN Analytics and the SA (slides 26 and 27); high CPU is an infrastructure matter, monitored by FOCOM, with TE&IV locating what is involved (slides 32 and 35); the new O-DU version enters through Software Package Onboarding, which admits NF packages, and the NFO coordinates the function update (slides 28 and 58); the extra capacity follows the flow in which the SO decides to expand, FOCOM shows the O-Cloud capacity and the NFO requests the scale-out over O2 (slides 29 to 31); and tracking KPIs uses the RAN NF OAM data reports, exposed by the DME to whoever needs them (slides 20, 21 and 25).

quiz.q: Producer or consumer? Situation A: RAN Analytics needs the data produced by another SMOS. Situation B: Policy Management needs to use a service offered by RAN Analytics. Situation C: a new SMOS enters the environment and needs to discover where a given service is.
quiz.a: The deck has no answer slide for this quiz (the next one, slide 13, is the architecture map), so there is no professor's answer key. What the deck itself indicates: A) RAN Analytics is a consumer of the data another SMOS produces; in the DME flow, the RAN NF OAM registers and produces the metrics and RAN Analytics discovers and consumes them (slides 20 and 21). B) Policy Management is the consumer and RAN Analytics is the producer of the service; it is the SME flow in which A (RAN Analytics) registers and B (Policy Management) needs to consume A (slide 17). C) The new SMOS acts as a consumer of the SME: discovering services is the consumer's role, and bootstrap helps new consumers find the initial endpoints (slide 16). Careful: on slide 10 the producer and consumer definitions appear swapped; use the meaning of slides 16 and 17 (the producer registers and offers, the consumer discovers and uses).

quiz.q: SME or DME? Situation A: I want to discover where a service is available. Situation B: I want to discover which performance metrics exist. Situation C: I want to authenticate a consumer of a service. Situation D: I want to make collected data available to an rApp. Situation E: I want to discover the endpoint of another SMOS.
quiz.a: Situation A: SME. Situation B: DME. Situation C: SME. Situation D: DME. Situation E: SME (slide 23). The criterion is the focus (slide 24): the SME handles services, with registration, service/endpoint discovery, and authentication and authorization of whoever accesses them (slide 16); the DME handles data, with data type registration, discovery of which data exist, and exposure of collected data to SMOFs and rApps (slide 19).

quiz.q: Who does what? Situation A: I need to instantiate a new O-DU. Situation B: I need to configure an O-DU that is already deployed. Situation C: I need to discover which clusters exist in the O-Cloud. Situation D: I need to know which resources are connected to a given O-DU. Situation E: I need to scale the deployment of an O-DU. Situation F: I need to discover the relationship between a site, an O-DU and the cloud resources.
quiz.a: Situation A: NFO. Situation B: RAN NF OAM. Situation C: FOCOM. Situation D: TE&IV. Situation E: NFO. Situation F: TE&IV (slide 39). Following the slide 42 table: instantiating and scaling are deployment lifecycle actions (NFO); configuring an already deployed NF is FCAPS operation (RAN NF OAM); discovering clusters is O-Cloud infrastructure inventory (FOCOM); and relationships between resources, sites and cloud are topology and relational inventory (TE&IV).

quiz.q: O-DU in trouble: who do you call? An O-DU shows degradation. The O-DU is configured but shows faults: which SMOS would you trigger? We find out the O-DU is consuming excessive resources and the deployment needs to be scaled: who steps in now? The cluster hosting the O-DU does not have enough capacity: whom do we need to query? We need to know which other resources and components are related to the O-DU: which SMOS would you trigger? So is there a single SMOS responsible for solving the problem?
quiz.a: Faults with the O-DU configured: RAN NF OAM. Deployment needs scaling: NFO. Cluster without capacity: FOCOM. Related resources and components: TE&IV. Is there a single responsible SMOS? NO (slide 41). The scenario on slides 26 and 27 shows the same chain: the OAM collects over O1, RAN Analytics and the SA detect the degradation, TE&IV points to what is involved, A1 Related takes the policy to the Near-RT RIC, the OAM applies persistent reconfiguration, and NFO and/or FOCOM step in if the cause is the deployment or the infrastructure.

quiz.q: SO or SA? Create a slice. Check whether the slice still meets the SLA. Choose where the slice components will be placed. Detect that latency exceeded the limit. Coordinate the delivery of the slice. Trigger remediation because the requirement is not being met.
quiz.a: Create a slice: SO. Check the SLA: SA. Choose the placement: SO. Detect latency above the limit: SA. Coordinate the delivery: SO. Trigger remediation: SA (slide 50). The SO executes the service or slice order, decides where deployments go and coordinates delivery (slide 43); the SA monitors, compares the current state with the required one and defines corrective actions when the requirement fails (slide 46). In the slide 48 scenario, the SA decides the action and the SO coordinates the execution of the remediation.

quiz.q: The slice is degrading! A factory has a RAN slice with a maximum latency of 10 ms, high reliability and guaranteed minimum throughput. After a few hours, latency rises to 18 ms. Who notices that the requirement is not being met? Who can help identify which NFs/sites are involved? Who can provide analysis of the indicators? What if the NF configuration needs to change? What if the deployment needs to be modified? What if the problem is related to the O-Cloud infrastructure? Who coordinates the delivery/orchestration of the service or slice?
quiz.a: Notices the violated requirement: SA. Identifies NFs/sites: TE&IV. Analyzes the indicators: RAN Analytics. Change the NF configuration: RAN NF OAM. Modify the deployment: NFO. O-Cloud infrastructure: FOCOM. Coordinates delivery/orchestration: SO (slide 54). It is the SA scenario of slides 47 and 48: the SA compares the 18 ms against the 10 ms limit, RAN Analytics points to the probable cause, TE&IV shows what is involved, the SO coordinates the remediation spread across OAM, NFO and FOCOM, and the SA escalates to the operator if the KPIs do not recover.
